title: Behind the Coats
passage:
A joint let go under the kitchen floor on a Sunday night, and for eight minutes none of the three adults living there could turn the water off. All three knew the tap under the sink was not it, and that there was an iron cover by the gate; none could say which side of the path. ___(1)___, they had lived there eleven years, which is long enough to have asked. The hall carpet took most of the damage.

There is nothing unusual in that house, and nothing modern about it either. In almost any house, one person knows which way the boiler override goes, which radiator to bleed first, which bin week it is. The knowledge holds no office and is not bought with the house. It may sit with the owner, the owner’s daughter, or the man who rents the back bedroom. Whoever has it is a ___(2)___: somebody who was in the right room on the right morning and has answered questions ever since.

This competence is not earned and not handed out. It is ___(3)___, the way a cold is, by being in the room when it happens. The fitter points a screwdriver at a valve and says “the one behind the coats”, and whoever is in the hall then has the fact for good – twenty years on, in the dark, first go. Nobody else will have it, because there is nothing in it to have: no rule, no principle, nothing that carries to another house. Each item is an ___(4)___. It names one thing in one building and explains nothing; most are four words long; nobody disputes them.

Nothing on that list is difficult and nothing on it is being kept back. Ask, and you will be told gladly and at length, and still have nothing. Although the whole of it is entirely ___(5)___, it moves one way only: one body pointing and another beside it, looking where the first points. A departure is therefore the dangerous event, and no household has a procedure for it. The woman who sold us this house talked for an hour on her last morning; I kept a fifth. What worked was the paint marker on her way out: an arrow on the boiler casing beside the override; on the third radiator, a ring round the bleed valve with a 1 in it.
– Felicity Endacott

questions.rationale: The gap takes Worse (D). What runs up to it is a pile of three failures – the tap under the sink is not it, the cover is by the gate somewhere, nobody can say which side of the path it is on – and the gapped sentence then adds a fact that makes those failures harder to forgive rather than easier: eleven years of living in the house, “which is long enough to have asked”. That relation is escalation, and only one of these four words marks it. Happily would turn the eleven years into a piece of luck, and the line straight afterwards refuses that reading: “The hall carpet took most of the damage”. Oddly would turn them into a surprise, and the second paragraph opens by denying surprise in terms: “There is nothing unusual in that house”. Nowadays would date the whole business to the present day, which that same opening also denies: “nothing modern about it either”. Each option is an adverb standing first in its sentence and followed by a comma, and the slot decides nothing on its own; three of the four then sit in that frame without strain, and Nowadays does not, because it puts the time in the present while the verb after the gap is in the past perfect. Among the three that do sit there, the only thing left to read is how the gapped sentence answers its predecessor.

The gap takes witness (A). The colon spells the person out and spells out nothing else: “somebody who was in the right room on the right morning”. A witness is one who was present when a thing happened, and being present is all this person ever did. Caretaker attaches a post with duties to the job, and this paragraph removed the post two lines earlier: “The knowledge holds no office”. Recruit makes the person somebody another person took on, which the defining clause rules out, because standing in a room on one morning is not a selection. Lodger fixes how the person occupies the building, and the line just in front of the gap deliberately leaves that open: “It may sit with the owner, the owner’s daughter, or the man who rents the back bedroom”. Four singular count nouns for a person in a house, one article between them, and all four read plainly before a colon, so nothing but sense can separate them.

The gap takes caught (B). The comparison inside the same sentence settles it: “the way a cold is, by being in the room when it happens”. Colds are caught, and they are caught by being there, which is precisely the claim this paragraph makes about the knowledge. Issued is refused by the line immediately in front of the gap: “This competence is not earned and not handed out”. Bought is refused by the paragraph above, which states where the knowledge does not come from: “The knowledge holds no office and is not bought with the house”. Chosen is turned away by the comparison itself, because nobody elects to have a cold, and by the clause that follows, where the fact falls to “whoever is in the hall then” rather than to anybody who put himself forward. Four past participles in one passive frame, each of which accepts the by-phrase that comes next, so the grammar of the slot settles nothing at all.

The gap takes address (A). The line that follows defines the missing noun: “It names one thing in one building and explains nothing”. Naming one thing and explaining none of it is what an address does, and no other word in this set does it. Instance needs a general kind to be an instance of, and the line in front of the gap says there is no such kind: “no rule, no principle, nothing that carries to another house”. Opinion would make the item arguable, and the defining line closes that off: “nobody disputes them”. Anecdote would make it a story, and a measurement in the same line forbids a story: “most are four words long”. Four singular nouns of one weight, each opening with a vowel so that the article in front of the gap discloses nothing, and each sitting in the frame without strain.

The gap takes commonplace (C). Although opens this sentence, so the adjective must pull against what comes next, which is that the knowledge “moves one way only”; a word for ordinariness is the only sort that pulls, because a thing anybody can say in four words ought to spread, and this knowledge will not. Technical is refused by the line in front of it: “Nothing on that list is difficult”. Privileged is refused by the other half of that line and by the one after it: “nothing on it is being kept back”, then “Ask, and you will be told gladly and at length”. Perishable is refused by the third paragraph, where the fact outlasts everybody: “twenty years on, in the dark, first go”. Three wrong answers on three separate grounds – difficulty, secrecy, and how long a thing lasts – and four adjectives of one weight in one predicative slot.

generator_meta.self_blind_solve: Stated honestly, and with the author's own blindness admitted: the passage and the gaps were designed together, so no figure below is an independent measurement. Two passes were run. (a) COVER THE PASSAGE. For each gap the four strings were laid out with the passage hidden and ranked on wording alone. Gap 1: four sentence adverbs, three of them -ly, on four different discourse relations; the only readable structure is the 3+1 stance cluster, whose off-axis member is a distractor; no route; 1-in-4. Gap 2: four singular nouns for people in a house, one article between them; the 3+1 standing cluster again points its odd member at a distractor; no route; 1-in-4. Gap 3: four six-letter past participles, exactly flat on length; the morphological odd one out is a distractor; no route; 1-in-4. Gap 4: four vowel-initial nouns of one weight; no route; 1-in-4. Gap 5: four adjectives, and the key is the longest by one character and the only compound, which is the one place a form reading could land; a blind solver who used it would score 1 here and 0 at gaps 1, 2 and 4, where the longest is a distractor. JOINT FLOOR ACROSS THE SHEET, options only: 5 x 0.25 = 1.25 of 5, which is 25 per cent, the base rate. The pick-the-longest heuristic scores 1.25 of 5 and the pick-the-shortest heuristic scores 1.25 of 5, both computed on the shipped strings; the pick-the-hedged and strip-the-absolutes heuristics return nothing at all. (b) RE-SOLVE FROM THE PASSAGE with the key list hidden. Each frame was read with all four candidates inserted in turn, and an argument was made FOR each wrong one before it was dropped. Gap 1's hardest rejection was Oddly, which an eleven-years fact really does invite until the next paragraph says in terms that there is nothing unusual in the house. Gap 2's hardest rejection was caretaker, kept longest because a household really does have somebody who looks after things, and refused on 'The knowledge holds no office'. Gap 3's hardest rejection was chosen, which the simile alone defeats. Gap 4's hardest rejection was instance, which is tempting because the paragraph is generalising - and which the same paragraph forbids, because an instance needs a kind and the text says there is no kind. Gap 5's hardest rejection was privileged, kept longest because one person really does hold the knowledge, and refused because holding is not withholding and the passage says so twice. Every gap came out single-answerable; no gap left two defensible options standing.
